reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Modern History
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: History Research Seminar
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: In the summer of 1809 the British sailed some 40,000 soldiers and 5,000 horses in 500 navy vessels over the English Channel to land in Walcheren. This greatest amphibious operation in Napoleonic times became know as the Walcheren Expedition or the Expedition to the Scheldt. The ultimate British goal was to occupy the important harbour of Antwerp. On the other side, Dutch and French forces, including many foreign troops like Irish, German and Polish were trying to stop the British assault. The outcome of the Walcheren Expedition not only left a big mark on local history, but also had an enormous impact on the Netherlands, France, Great Brittain and international politics in general. In this course we will research the primary sources about the Walcheren expedition. Think about diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports written by soldiers, officers or officials form all participants in this conflict. You will learn how to search for, read and analyse these primary sources, through writing a course-filling paper; as such, this course will require a lot of self-study and fewer class meetings.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: Primary-source Walcheren Expedition research; German troops occur incidentally. No German-studies sequence.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Principles of Private Law
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: Life comprises a variety of situations in which private law plays a role . Simply considering the home implicates several complex relationships: family relatives , landlords and tenants, neighbors. Stepping out the front door leads to a further range of transactions that can have legal consequences for those involved. The rights and obligations associated with relationships and transactions among (natural and legal) persons are largely determined by a collection of legal areas known collectively as private law. This course introduces students to principles of selected fields of private law, and students will closely examine property law, tort law, contract law, and other legal areas. The overarching principles within each of these fields will be illuminated using a comparative law approach, considering primarily the legal systems of Germany, France, England, China, and the United States of America. Additionally, students will be challenged to consider private law concepts in broader contexts. Building on the skills acquired in GOSLAWJ101 and other UCR law track courses , this course on private law will seek to uncover the latent social, economic, and political pressures underlying many of the legal principles that will be discussed.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: Comparative private law includes Germany among five systems; no German language/linguistics/literature content.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: European Union Politics
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: EU institutions, interest groups and legislative dossier research; European context cannot replace German disciplinary substance.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Psycholinguistics
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: Neuroscience, acquisition, bilingualism and comprehension of language; one 7.5-EC course, not German proficiency or a German linguistics sequence. Requires HCBGATE102.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Dutch
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: Basic Dutch daily communication, not German.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Style & Meaning
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: The Style and Meaning course is firmly grounded in stylistics, which is the study of style in texts. Stylistics involves identifying and analysing the linguistic choices that serve to create meaning in texts. Originally an outgrowth of the third canon of classical rhetoric (elocutio), and later heavily influenced by movements in twentieth and twenty-first century linguistics, modern stylistics has grown into a recognizable discipline in its own right, with its own distinct theories and practices. While stylistics can be used to analyse any type of text, traditionally the discipline has been most concerned with the style of literary texts. As such, stylistics has sometimes been referred to as ‘literary stylistics’ or ‘literary linguistics.’ The course textbook also works almost exclusively with fictional texts to introduce and illustrate theoretical concepts and frameworks and their application. Nonetheless, further in-class application will at times extend beyond the fictional and students will be allowed to choose non-fictional texts for their instruction presentations and term papers. Students will be invited to consider the linguistic choices made by (literary) writers by reflecting on why certain linguistic strategies may be more effective than others in achieving particular interpretive effects. Students will be asked to consider all levels of language from the phonetic to the discoursal, to the cognitive. Therefore, an interest in language is crucial to this course.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: Literary stylistics provides close analysis, not sustained German-language literary study.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Rhetoric in Action
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: Dutch/English community work teaching children rhetoric, not German didactics or teacher certification.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: Poetry, performance and creative practice, not advanced German writing.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Great Literary Works
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: This course is based on a selection of major literary texts which should be considered essential for every LAS student’s cultural capital: texts that for centuries have inspired Western culture, visual arts and theatre, and which resonate themes that preoccupy social sciences and philosophy. The course is a chronological overview of literature ranging from the earliest monuments (the epic of Gilgamesh) to post-modernity. Within this framework students will read primary (literary) and secondary (critical, theoretical) texts debating what it means to be human, mortal, female, male, or child, or what it means to be responsible, free, a member of family or other community, to be civilized or barbarian. What makes literature different from anecdote? Why are some children’s texts indebted to philosophical tale? Probing these and many other questions, students will be invited to analyse literary representations of home, labour, leisure, duty, love, leadership, organized religion, and memory, and try to correlate these topics with various artistic forms used by writers. In this way the course is an encounter with diverse genres: heroic epic, philosophical tale, fairy tale, short story, autobiography, essay and novella. With this broad approach to themes and forms in the Western literary heritage, the course is an alternative introduction to literary studies, and of fundamental value to everyone interested in literary and cultural studies.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: World Myth & Literature
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: How do ancient literary myths compare to the literature of other parts of the world? What can these parallels tell us about age-old global connections, or even about universal human themes? This course explores what might be tentatively named the literary silk road, but also taps into the narrative traditions of continents beyond. For instance, we investigate the similarities between the stories of ancient epic poems, from Homer to Virgil, with the Indian epic Mahabharata; we look at the strands between the romance novels of the classical world and those from Byzantine and Arabic literature. We explore how storytelling is expressed beyond text, for instance in oral traditions, visual culture, or in theatrical performance. The tradition of depicting mythical narratives is common to cultures all over the world. What are the processes of transmitting text into image? How do these literary images differ across cultures? Spanning four millennia and at least three continents, this course will examine how literary stories of myth form a deep cultural foundation, and how they deal with universal human themes like love, loyalty, power, and friendship.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Life & Travel Writing
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: The course is devoted to various forms of life narrative in literature and popular culture such as memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel narrative as well as blog. It prepares students to read and analyse them, and be sensitive to autobiographical modes in the media. Through this critical encounter with life storying students are encouraged to develop a critical awareness of the postmodern ‘culture of autobiography’ (Folkenflik, R. The Culture of Autobiography. Stanford UP, 1993). In the course, students will build up their writing, presentation and debating skills, and their critical self-reflection. They will be invited to prove their comprehension of crucial theoretical aspects of life narrative research referring to their own individual experience and applying their creative writing skills in order to produce structured personal narratives. With its broadly conceived approach to life narrative studied in the context of large cultural processes, the course ideally fits the paradigm of liberal arts.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Film & Text
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: It is a researched fact that more than 50% of films have their literary originals. More than three-quarters of the American Academy Awards have been granted to films based on novels, short stories and dramas. There are plentiful examples of famous films based on no less famous literary texts, from the already hackneyed Pride and Prejudice, through Bridget Jones’ Diary, The Lord of the Rings, the Narnia cycle, A Passage to India, Batman, A Thousand and One Nights to Frankenstein, Dracula, Ninety Eighty-Four and Hamlet. This close relation between literature and film becomes even clearer when we realize that film is a text that tells a story. Keeping this in mind, in this course we will discuss various ways in which a literary original is translated on screen, tracing various links between literary and film narration, and various intertextual dimensions of film adaptation. The course offers instruction in a methodology of film analysis, building on students’ knowledge of literature, media and popular culture. As it studies manifold transactions between the adaptor, the critic and the viewers, it is vital to every student interested in literature, media, popular culture and journalism. Our first step is the basic formalist analysis of a literary text along with its plot, structure, character, setting, and a formalist analysis of the multi-track film (image, acting, music, sound effects) along with its “syntax” and “diction” which all contribute to its tone and themes.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Introduction to Film & Media
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: MCCMED111: Introduction to Film & Media provides you with a solid foundation in the study of film, while also introducing you briefly to media more broadly. The course begins by tracing the development of cinema from its earliest experiments to later artistic movements and innovations. This historical perspective helps you understand film not only as entertainment but also as an evolving cultural form that reflects and shapes society. At the same time, we focus on the elements of film form, such as narrative, cinematography, editing, and sound, which give you the vocabulary needed to describe and analyze how films work. Much of our attention is on film culture and analysis, since these provide the best starting point for further study in the field. Together, we examine and discuss influential examples, considering both their artistic qualities and their broader theoretical and political contexts. This approach allows you to see how films respond to social change while also experimenting with style and technique. In the final part of the course, we widen our perspective to take a short look at media more generally. By considering examples from television, streaming, and digital platforms, we make connections between film and the wider media environment and prepare the ground for more advanced courses in the cluster. Engagement with academic readings is another central part of the course. These texts present important concepts and debates that shape the study of film and media.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Media Archaeology
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: Media Archaeology explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies, such as cassette tapes, typewriters, and early printed books, and how they shaped the production, circulation, and preservation of knowledge. We will study these objects from multiple perspectives, combining close material analysis with broader historical and cultural interpretation. You will examine how physical properties such as weight, texture, and durability influence communication and memory. The course will include seminar discussions, critical reflections, and hands-on activities that encourage active engagement with obsolete media. Practical exercises may involve recording silence, identifying the sonic characteristics of cassette hiss, or investigating the design, use, and cultural impact of the Sony Walkman. Through these activities, we will learn to treat media as both historical evidence and lived experience, linking material form to cultural meaning. These media objects are chosen because they exemplify the theories and readings central to debates in media archaeology today. By the end of the semester, you will have developed analytical thinking, interpretive skill, and cultural awareness consistent with the aims of a liberal arts education. You will be able to explain how studying obsolete and pre-digital technologies informs our understanding of today’s media. No technical expertise is required, only curiosity and a willingness to work closely with media as physical and cultural artifacts.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: From T.V. to TikTok
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: This course examines social history and everyday life through American mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Its central premise is threefold. First, storytelling shapes how we understand the world. Second, who gets to tell the story matters. Third, media provides insight into the past, present, and constructions for possible futures. Engaging with narratives across a wide range of media, from television and film to podcasts and TikTok, supports this point. So does amplifying the voices of the silenced and treating viral moments, such as a Justin Bieber performance clip, as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values, anxieties, and desires. The course opens with fear, conformity, and identity, using The Twilight Zone (1959) and Black Mirror (2011–) as bookends of the same uneasy question: what does society do to the individual? Week two then draws from future foresight methodology to explore the question: what does society imagine for itself in the future? Who is centered and who left out of the imaginations? The course then turns to mediated constructions of "reality," placing competing versions of the same story side by side and asking who the narrative serves and who it harms. Case studies include the "Hollywood Indian" versus films written, directed, and acted by Native Americans. The juxtaposition exposes how the media both marginalizes and empowers. A parallel examination of disability representation contrasts the inspirational "disabled hero" trope with authentic portrayals by differently abled people themselves.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Media & the Environment
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: Media and the Environment examines how environmental issues are represented and debated through visual and audiovisual media. You study how media shape the ways ecological problems are understood, felt, and acted upon. The course introduces key concepts such as the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested ideas of nature, and indigenous and postcolonial media. You use these concepts as analytical tools to examine how environmental meaning is produced across different media forms and cultural contexts. The main goal of the course is to help you analyze environmental media critically and precisely. You learn how film, photography, sound, and digital media make ecological processes, environmental risk, and human and nonhuman relations visible and intelligible. The course emphasizes close analysis of images, narratives, and aesthetic strategies, as well as comparison across media genres and historical moments. You also examine how media translate scientific knowledge and lived experience into stories, images, and affects that shape public understanding, sustainability discourse, and political judgment. Questions of agency, scale, temporality, and responsibility guide your analysis throughout the course. The course combines sustained reading with structured discussion and applied analytical work. You work with scholarly texts, media examples, and guided exercises, and you complete either a final analytical paper or a media-based project. This combination reflects the core idea of the course.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: Media & Race
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: Whose stories are remembered and whose are erased? What do the stories un/told teach us about power, privilege, and resistance? How do cultural expressions and forms like film, photographs, and music address systemic racism, critique the present, and envision just futures? These questions steer this course. Addressing them reveals links between past and present that students explore in final podcasts grounded in research and fueled by passion. Race, at the heart of American history and life, is at the center of this class. We begin in the late 19th century with the “end” of slavery and continue into the 21st century with the advent of ICE. Throughout the term we explore the ways media supports systems of oppression and empowers the oppressed.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.

reviewedAdjacentCourses.name: The Documentary
reviewedAdjacentCourses.actualContent: In this course we will discuss the development of the documentary form and discover various techniques used by documentary film makers. We start by tracing the documentary film from its origins (e.g. including the work of pioneer documentarians like Dziga Vertov and Robert Flaherty) to the present. We will analyze a large number of non-fiction representations of the world and its people, focusing on a range of documentary styles and genres and rooting this diversity in its various historical and social contexts, as well as considering the ethical and aesthetic aspects of documentaries. The course primarily considers documentary film, but we will also explore the genre through other media forms, including audio productions, allowing students to develop skills useful in an increasingly multimodal culture. Assessment includes a presentation, the production of a very short documentary item, an essay-type exam and several small homework assignments on Moodle. Input to help shape this course is highly appreciated.
reviewedAdjacentCourses.judgment: General literary/film analysis or broader modern history has adjacent intellectual value but does not establish German-language proficiency, specialist German literature/linguistics or compulsory German-speaking immersion.
